en: The Dignified Conduct of a Śrāmaṇera, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Jibin during the Song Dynasty.
Having already received the ten śrāmaṇera precepts, one becomes a worthy practitioner of the Way. Next, one should be taught what is to be practiced, gradually.
Accumulation begins from what is small.
One should know the proper deportment and practices;
one should know the age of the preceptor and the names of the three teachers.
One should be taught to recognize the number of years, months, and days since first receiving the precepts;

one should know how many matters pertain to serving the *upādhyāya*, as well as how many matters pertain to following the *ācārya*; one should also know how many matters pertain to providing tooth-sticks and water for washing, how many matters pertain to handing over the *kāṣāya* and holding the alms bowl, and how many matters pertain to grasping the *khakkhara* staff and carrying the sandals.

When one is together with one’s preceptor (upādhyāya) and teacher (ācārya) during times of invitation—whether arriving at the house of a king, the house of a Kṣatriya, or the house of a Brahmin; whether eating while seated together or eating while seated separately;
whether entering the city together to beg for alms or returning together to the original place;
or whether eating by the water’s edge at the end of the day or eating together under a tree; [in all such cases, they should act in concert].
If one departs beforehand and waits for the other;
if they combine their bowls to eat; if they exchange bowls;
if it is the time for facing the meal; or if it is the time for eating before or after [the formal meal].
Whether it be at the time of washing and rinsing after the meal, or when departing with the bowl washed;
or if one is to serve as the appointed attendant for the Sangha, one should know that there are certain matters regarding this service that must be understood. What are these matters?
When one who has reached twenty years of age desires to receive the precepts, all these matters must be thoroughly investigated and known.
Even if he is a worthy person, if he does not fully answer the questions posed by the bhikṣus, the full ordination (upasampadā) should not be granted to him.
Why is this? One who acts as a śrāmaṇera does not even know what a śrāmaṇera should practice.
The duties of a śramaṇa are great and difficult to perform; they are exceedingly subtle and profound.
"Virtuous śrāmaṇera!
You should depart for now and study thoroughly; once you have heard and understood everything, you shall then receive full ordination.
The reason you do not yet know all the matters pertaining to a śrāmaṇera is that you must come together with us to understand them clearly, for it is through bodily goodness that one attains this."
It is simply that you do not understand and do not submit your will.

Yet you now wish to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) once again; I shall now confer the full ordination upon you. People say that the Buddha-dharma is easy to practice and that being a śramaṇa is easy to become, but they do not realize how profound the Way of the Buddha is, nor how the operations of sin and merit and the laws of discipline interact with one another.
Because one must examine them frequently during this period, one should first inquire [about their suitability].
If the candidate’s responses are complete and conform to the Dharma, it will be easy to find the three masters.
There are five matters regarding the instruction of a śrāmaṇera by the master:
First, one should revere the Great Śramaṇa;
second, one must not address the Great Śramaṇa by name;
third, when the Great Śramaṇa recites the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, one must not eavesdrop.
Fourth, one must not seek out the faults of a *mahābhikṣu*;
fifth, when a *mahābhikṣu* errs, one must not speak of it by way of circumlocution.
These constitute the rules of dignified conduct (*airyāpathika-dharma*).
One should be instructed to practice five matters:
first, one must not revile a great bhikṣu in private;
second, one must not treat a great bhikṣu with contempt, nor mock them by imitating their speech, appearance, or gait in their presence.
Third, if one sees a great bhikṣu passing by, one should rise and stand, or if one is reciting a sūtra;
however, if one is eating or performing communal duties, one should not rise.
Fourth, if one encounters a great bhikṣu while walking, one should stop and move to a lower path to yield passage.
Fifth, if one is being frivolous or sees a great bhikṣu, one should immediately cease and apologize, saying that one was not aware.
This is what should be practiced accordingly.
There are ten matters regarding a śrāmaṇera’s service to his preceptor:
First, one should rise early;
second, when wishing to enter a room, one should first snap one's fingers three times;
third, one should prepare tooth-sticks and water for rinsing.
Fourth, one should first present the *kāṣāya* and then present the sandals;
fifth, one should sweep the floor and replenish the water for washing;
sixth, one should clear away dust and wipe down the beds and mats.
Seventh, while the teacher has gone out and not yet returned, one must not leave the dwelling midway; when the teacher returns, one should go forward to receive his *kāṣāya* and fold it inwardly.
Eighth, if there is a transgression, and the *upādhyāya* or *ācārya* instructs and admonishes one, one must not respond with contrary words.
Ninth, one should depart after bowing the head to receive the teacher’s words, and one should contemplate and keep them in mind to put them into practice.
Tenth: when leaving the room, one should pull the door shut behind oneself.
These are the rules for serving the upādhyāya.
There are five matters regarding a śrāmaṇera’s service to an ācārya:
First, you must regard the ācārya in every respect as you would me;
second, you must not engage in frivolous play;
third, even if he should scold or revile you, you must not retort.
Fourth, if one is made to carry out impure vessels, one must not spit upon them nor harbor anger, malice, or resentment;
fifth, when lodging at night, one should perform self-massage.
These are the rules for attending upon an ācārya.
When a śrāmaṇera serves his teacher, he should rise early and prepare tooth-sticks and water for rinsing; there are six matters regarding this:
first, when cutting and breaking the tooth-sticks, they should be of the proper length;
second, one should split the tip.
Third, one should wash them until they are clean;
fourth, one should replace the old water that has been kept overnight;
fifth, one should cleanse the water jar.
Sixth, one should enter carrying a vessel filled with water, ensuring it makes no sound.
This is the method for providing tooth-sticks and bathing water.
There are four matters regarding the bestowing of the *kāṣāya*:
First, one should slowly take hold of the lower part with one hand and offer it to him;
second, one should then look at both the upper and lower parts;
third, one should properly stand while holding the teacher's robe.
Fourth, one should place it over the shoulder;
this is the dharma of the kāṣāya.
There are four matters regarding the folding of the kāṣāya:
First, one should look at the space above and below;
second, one must not allow it to touch the ground;
third, one should place it in its regular location.
Fourth, fold it over the top.
This is the method for folding the kāṣāya.
There are four matters regarding the holding of the alms bowl:
First, one should wash it until it is clean;
second, wipe it until it is dry;
third, fasten it so that it is secure.
Fourth, one must not make any sound.
These are the rules for carrying the alms-bowl.
There are four matters regarding the carrying of sandals:
First, one should shake it out;
second, one should inspect it and fold it properly;
third, one should wash one's hands before handling the kāṣāya; one must not hold it immediately.
Fourth, when the teacher is seated, one should take up [the sandals] and place them in order beside him.
This is the method for maintaining the sandals.
There are four matters regarding the maintenance of the *khakkhara* (staff):
First, one should take it and wipe away any fresh impurities;
second, one should take it without placing it on the ground so that it makes a sound;
third, one should present it only after the teacher has stepped out of the door.

Fourth, when the teacher returns from outside, one should go out to meet him and take [the staff]; whether traveling together, entering the assembly, or prostrating before the Buddha, one should take it up and carry it.
This is the method for carrying the khakkhara staff.
When invited to sit together for a meal, there are four matters to observe:
first, when seated, one should remain six feet away from the teacher;
second, one should wait until the teacher has finished his great almsgiving before offering him the bowl.
Third, one must not eat before the teacher;
fourth, having finished eating, one should rise and take the bowl to oneself.
These are the rules for the mealtime concerning sitting in a row.
There are four rules for the method of sitting apart from the meal:
first, one should stand beside the teacher;
second, one should only sit down and depart after being instructed to do so regarding the meal.
Third, one should prostrate with the head and face touching the ground;
fourth, when leaving the meal, one must not sit back arrogantly or play about.
When the meal is finished, one should go to stand beside the teacher; only when the teacher instructs one to return to one's seat should one sit.
This is the rule for when one is eating while seated separately.
When entering a city to beg for food, there are four matters:
first, one should carry the teacher’s alms bowl;
Second, one should follow [the teacher] and must not step on the teacher’s shadow with one's feet;
third, when outside the city, one should take up the bowl and present it to the teacher;
fourth, when entering the city and intending to go elsewhere, one should inform the teacher.
This is the method for practicing alms-gathering.
Upon returning together to the original place, there are four matters to be observed during the mealtime:
first, one should first slowly open the door and spread out the sitting mats.
Second, having washed the teacher’s hands, one then withdraws to wash one's own;
third, having offered the bowl to the teacher, one then withdraws to stand with palms joined;
fourth, one should prepare in advance the soap powder and hand-towel.
This is the method for returning to eat at the time of the meal.
When returning to the water's edge to eat, there are four matters:
first, one should seek out a clean place.
Second, one should seek out grass to make a seat;
third, one should take water to wash the teacher’s hands and then present the bowl;
fourth, when the teacher instructs one to eat, one should perform a prostration and then sit down.
This is the rule for eating by the water's edge.
When eating while staying under a tree, there are four matters to attend to:
first, take the bowl and place it on a branch, then gather leaves to make a seat.
Second, upon returning from fetching water, one should wash the teacher’s hands; if no water is available, one should seek out pure grass and offer it to the teacher.
Third, one should return to take the teacher’s bowl and present it to him.
Fourth, one should prepare pure grass in advance, and having cleansed the teacher’s bowl, one should wipe it thoroughly before departing.
This is the rule for the mealtime under a tree.
When waiting for one another while on the road, there are three matters:
first, holding the bowl, placing it on clean ground, and performing a prostration as previously described.
Second, one should observe whether it is early or late in the day to determine whether to return home or continue on the road;
third, one should take up the teacher’s bowl and follow behind him.
These are the rules for mutual conduct while traveling on the road.
When eating from a shared bowl, there are three matters to attend to:
first, if there is no curd, ghee, or gruel in the teacher’s bowl, one should take the bowl one has received and offer it to the teacher;
if the teacher does not accept it, one should simply step back and wait.
Second, he slowly took half of the rice from his bowl and placed it upon a tree leaf.
Third, he then took half of the rice from his own bowl and placed it into his teacher’s bowl, and stood back.
This is the rule for eating from a shared bowl.
When exchanging bowls, there are three matters:
first, if one obtains something superior from the teacher’s bowl while taking something inferior for oneself, one should immediately offer it back to the teacher.
Second, if the teacher wishes to trade for the bowl, one should decline and not accept it;
third, if the teacher insists on trading for the bowl, one may take one or two mouthfuls of food, then wipe the bowl and return it to the teacher.
This is the rule for exchanging alms bowls.
When facing the teacher during the meal, there are three matters to attend to:
first, one should present the teacher’s bowl and then withdraw to eat from one's own.
Second, one should frequently observe what the teacher wishes to receive, and immediately rise to take it and offer it;
third, when eating, one should neither be too hurried nor too slow, and once one has risen, one should again ask, "What would you like?"
The teacher says, "Take it," and then one should take it.
This is the rule for the time of receiving food.
There are three matters regarding the times before and after the meal:
First, having taken up the teacher’s bowl and utensils, one should withdraw to a secluded place and wait; upon hearing the teacher’s call, one should immediately respond.
Second, one should beforehand take water for washing and set it aside.

Third, when the teacher has finished eating, one should wash the teacher’s hands and then step back; only when the teacher instructs one to remove the food should one perform a prostration and remove the food.
This is the procedure for the time before and after the meal.
Once the meal is finished, there are three matters regarding washing and rinsing:
first, having washed and rinsed, one should first take the teacher’s bowl, wash it until it is clean, and place it upon a tree leaf.

Second, after having washed one’s own bowl, one should also place it upon a tree leaf; first taking the teacher’s bowl, rub it with the hand until dry, place it inside the bag, and present it to the teacher.
Third, return and take up one’s own bowl, wipe it until dry, place it inside the bag, and carry it while staying there.
This is the rule for washing the bowl.
When departing after washing the bowl, there are three things to do:
first, one should say, "I now wish to go to such-and-such a place to visit the venerable [name]."
Second, one should prostrate with the head and face touching the ground and then depart;
third, one should return alone;
one must not pass through other villages laughing or playing.
Return directly to your original place to recite the sūtras;
this is the rule for departing after washing the bowl.
There are five matters regarding a śrāmaṇera entering the assembly:
First, one should clearly study;
second, one should practice various tasks;
third, one should provide for the community.
Fourth, one should bestow the requisites of a great śramaṇa;
fifth, when one wishes to receive the full precepts, it is easy to find the three masters.
Furthermore, there are five other matters:
First, one should pay homage to the Buddha;
second, one should pay homage to the community of bhikṣus;
third, one should inquire after the health of the senior monks.
Fourth, one should leave space for the position of the senior monk;
fifth, one must not dispute over the seating place.
Furthermore, there are five other matters:
First, one must not call out to or laugh with others from afar while seated;
second, one must not rise and leave frequently;
third, if the community of monks calls for a novice by name, saying "Novice So-and-so," one must immediately rise and respond.
Fourth, one should follow the instructions and commands of the Sangha;
fifth, if the *karmadāna* (monastic administrator) calls one to perform some task, one should return and inform one's teacher.
These constitute the rules for entering the assembly.
A śrāmaṇera serving as the day-duty officer has five matters to attend to:
first, he must cherish the property of the Saṃgha;
second, he must not perform his tasks in the middle of the path.
Third, once a task has begun but is not yet finished, one must not abandon it midway and depart;
fourth, if the upādhyāya or ācārya calls for you, you must not go immediately, but should instead inform the karmadāna;
fifth, you must follow the instructions and commands of the karmadāna and must not act in opposition or contravention.
This is the method for serving as the duty officer.
There are five matters regarding the selection of vegetables:
first, one must remove the roots.
Second, the edges should be even;
third, one must not allow green and yellow parts to be mixed together;
fourth, when washing vegetables, one should change the water three times to ensure they are clean, and once cleaned, one should shake them three times to remove the water.
Fifth, when a task has been completed, one should return and sweep it clean.
Furthermore, there are five other matters:
first, one must not privately take property belonging to the Sangha.
Second, if there is anything one wishes to take, one should inform the *karmadāna*;
third, one should perform the affairs of the Sangha to the best of one's ability;
fourth, one should sweep the dining hall and then arrange empty tables within it.
Fifth, one should sweep behind the dwelling and replenish the water supply both morning and evening.
There are ten matters regarding the drawing of water:
first, if the hands are not clean, one must not immediately use them to draw water; one should first wash the hands.
Second, one must not throw the bucket into the well with force so that it makes a sound;
third, one should lower the bucket slowly and must not strike it against the sides of the well with force so that it makes a sound;
fourth, one must not allow the end of the rope to slip back into the well.
Fifth, one must not carry footwear while leaning against a well-railing;
sixth, one must not pour water from a jar directly into a cauldron;
seventh, one must not set a jar down on the ground.
Eighth, one should wash the bathing vessel until it is clean;
ninth, when carrying water inside, one should proceed slowly;
tenth, one should place it in a secluded spot and not obstruct the path of people.
There are five matters regarding the washing of the cauldron:
first, one should first wash the upper rim of the cauldron;
second, one should wash the interior of the cauldron.
Third, one should wash the middle of the waist and the abdomen;
fourth, one should wash the inner bottom;
fifth, one should change the water three times for each.
There are five matters regarding blowing on a stove:
first, one must not squat while blowing on the fire;
second, one must not ignite raw wood.
Third, one must not blow on wet firewood upside down;
fourth, one must not burn rotten firewood;
fifth, one must not extinguish the fire by pouring hot water over it.
There are five matters regarding the sweeping of the floor:
first, one should sweep in the direction of the grain;
second, when sprinkling water on the ground, it must not be applied unevenly.
Third, one must not soil or splash the four walls;
fourth, one must not tread upon damp ground and thereby damage the floor;
fifth, having finished sweeping, one should immediately sort the grass oneself and discard it.
When a bhikṣu-saṃgha is eating and a śrāmaṇera sweeps the ground, there are five matters to observe:
first, one must walk backward;
second, one must not swing one's arms or hands.
Third, when more than six people are present, they should stop and form a single group;
fourth, one should sweep everywhere thoroughly for the sake of goodness;
fifth, one should immediately remove it with one's own hands, carry it out, and discard it.
There are five matters regarding the pouring of water from a water-vessel (*kuṇḍikā*):
First, one hand shall hold the top and the other hand the bottom; they must not be switched.
Second, one should remain close to the left side, holding [the vessel] firmly and gazing straight ahead.
Third, one should observe the person’s hand when pouring water; it must be neither too much nor too little, but poured directly into the person’s hand.
Fourth, when pouring the water, it should be held four inches away from the person’s hand—neither higher nor lower—and one should observe the quantity of water;
if there is not enough for one person, one should add more, but one must not let the water remain in the person’s hand.
Fifth, having washed one's hands, one returns to put on the *kāṣāya*.
There are five matters regarding the carrying of the wash-basin:
first, one must not allow the basin to make a sound.
Second, one should hold it firmly with both hands and lean it against the right side [of the body];
third, one should follow the height of the person's hand and must not look left or right;
fourth, when the basin is full, one should pour out the water and discard it, and must not pour it onto the ground in front of others.
Fifth, having finished washing one's hands, one should put on the *kāṣāya* again.
There are five matters regarding the hand-towel:
first, one should hold the upper end with the right hand and the lower end with the left hand, and offer one end to the person [receiving it].
Second, one should sit two chi away; one must not lean forward against another's knee.
Third, one should hold the towel and must not use it to obstruct another’s mouth.

Fourth, while another person is wiping themselves and has not yet released the towel, one must not pull it away; once the task is finished, one should return it to its owner or place it back in its original location.
Fifth, having washed one's hands, one should return to put on the *kāṣāya*.
There are five matters regarding the bestowing of sandals:
first, one should first shake them out to remove whatever is inside.
Second, one should rise from one's seat upon seeing the senior monk;
third, one should follow behind the bowl-washer to show the host the way so that he may recognize [the vessel];
fourth, one must not place the left hand on the right side; in all such matters, one should act as a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) would.
Fifth, when the meal is finished, one should wash one's hands and put on the *kāṣāya* again.
There are seven matters concerning the *śrāmaṇera*'s bowl:
first, if there is leftover rice in the bowl, one must not simply take it up and discard it.
Second, when one wishes to discard rice, it should be placed on clean ground;
third, one should use cleansing beans or grass leaves;
fourth, when washing the bowl, one must not do so on clean ground or in a place frequented by people.
Fifth, when washing the bowl, one must provide a stand for it;
sixth, one must replenish it with fresh water, and the used water must not be discarded too far away so as to splash and soil the ground;
seventh, when wishing to pour out the water from the bowl, one should hold it four inches above the ground, neither higher nor lower.
There are three matters regarding the wiping of the alms bowl:
first, one should wash one's hands and wipe [the bowl] until it is dry;
second, one should hold a clean hand-towel and place it upon one's knees.
Third, one should wipe the interior until it is dry, then cover it with a clean cloth and place it inside its bag, storing it in its usual location.
When attending a meal gathering, there are five matters regarding instructing a śrāmaṇera to hold the bowl:
first, one must not place it on the ground;
Second, one must not stack them so that they make a sound;
third, when requesting someone to set them down, one must ensure they touch the ground;
fourth, until another person has handed over the bowl, one must not place it upon a table.
Fifth, one must not receive the bowl from behind another person; it should be received directly from the front, nor from within the assembly.
Once you have observed that the teacher has finished eating, you should rise, take the bowl, and return to your seat.
When a śrāmaṇera carries a letter for his preceptor to deliver as a reply of thanks to someone, there are seven matters to observe:
first, he should go directly;
second, he should return directly.
Third, one should remember what the teacher says, as well as the responses given by others;
fourth, one must not pass through places recklessly;
fifth, if one has borrowed anything, one must not remain there overnight.
Sixth, one must not be frivolous or deceitful;
seventh, when going out, one must act according to the proper rules.
While a śrāmaṇera is still performing tasks for the community of monks, he must not enter the gate of the Great Śramaṇa’s quarters at will.
There are three circumstances under which one may enter:
first, when the preceptor or ācārya temporarily sends one on an errand;
second, when one is commissioned to fetch something.
Third, when one goes personally to inquire about the sutras, one should be permitted to enter.
There are seven matters regarding the desire to enter a room:
first, one must snap the fingers three times before being allowed to enter.
Second, one must not perform it facing toward people;
third, one must not speak of other matters frivolously;
fourth, one must join the palms and speak according to the Dharma.
Fifth, one should not teach with an air of arrogance nor cross one's legs;
sixth, one must not engage in frivolous chatter or derision;
seventh, one must not obstruct others who are ahead; when wishing to exit, one should turn back and pull the door.
When sending a śrāmaṇera on a journey alone, you should instruct him that there are three matters regarding the superior [the preceptor]:
first, if someone asks you, "What is your preceptor's name? you should reply, "My preceptor’s name is so-and-so."
Second, he asked again, "How many years has your preceptor been a śramaṇa? He replied, "For so many years.
Third, he asked again, "Where is your preceptor from? He replied, "He is a native of such-and-such a commandery and county."
If one further asks, "What is the name of your preceptor? one should reply, "His name is so-and-so.
If one further asks, "How old is your preceptor? one should reply, "He is such-and-such years of age."
He asked again, "Where is the Ācārya from? and the reply was, "I am a man from such-and-such a commandery.
If he were to ask again, "Where are you, O worthy one, from? the reply would be, "I am a man from such-and-such a commandery and district."
He asked again, "What is the name of the worthy one? and he replied, "My name is so-and-so.
He asked again, "How long has it been since you became a śrāmaṇera? and he replied, "It has been such a number of years, such months and days, and such seasons."
This is how one recognizes one's preceptor and ācārya, as well as knowing the time, the year, the month, and the number of days.
There are five matters regarding entering the bathhouse:
first, one should enter with the head bowed.
Second, one must avoid occupying the seat of a senior elder;
third, when a senior elder recites the scriptures, one must not speak frivolously;
fourth, one must not wash one another with water.
Fifth, one must not extinguish fire by pouring water upon it.
Furthermore, there are five other matters:
first, one must not engage in mocking or derisive speech.
Second, one must not break the large jars or pots;
third, one must not waste water;
fourth, one must not soil the bathing beans or sesame oil within them.
Fifth, once one has gone out, one must not stop to wash clothes.
Upon reaching the area behind the dwellings, there are ten matters:
first, when one wishes to defecate or urinate, one should go immediately.
Second, while walking, one must not look to the left or right;
third, upon arrival, one should snap the fingers three times;
fourth, one must not urge others to leave.
Fifth, once you have arrived, you must snap your fingers three times;
sixth, you must not swallow loudly;
seventh, you must not lower your head to look at your private parts.
Eighth, one must not play with the dust and ash above;
ninth, one must not take water and pour it upon the walls;
tenth, once finished, one should wash one's hands; until they have been washed, one must not handle any objects.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, one must not spit directly against the front wall;
second, one must not look around to the left or right.
Third, one must not take grass and draw on the ground;
fourth, one must not take a fire-torch and draw on the ground or on walls;
fifth, one must not remain for long; having ascended, one should descend quickly.
If one encounters people, one must not perform a salutation, but should yield the path and avoid them.
There are ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras;
the first is that all sentient beings exist because of food and drink.
Second, the two truths;
third, the three feelings;
fourth, the four truths;
Fifth, the five aggregates;
sixth, the six sense bases;
seventh, the seven factors of enlightenment.
Eighth, the Eightfold Noble Path;
ninth, the nine abodes of sentient beings;
tenth, the ten totalities.
These are called the ten numbers. First, the novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*):
he has resolved his mind to leave secular life, for he cherishes and wears the Way within his breast.
Second, they destroy their physical beauty in order to adopt the Dharma robes;
third, they sever all ties of affection forever so as not to harbor attachment;
fourth, they cast aside their bodies and lives in order to honor and follow the Way.
Fifth, they aspire to seek the Mahāyāna for the sake of delivering all beings.
"I respectfully address the assembly of virtuous monks seated in the four directions!
The śrāmaṇera [Name], together with these many others, prostrates and pays homage."

I have heard that when the Great Sun hangs its halo, all living beings are bathed in clarity; when the True Honored One expounds the teachings, those with sincere hearts attain awakening. When the multitude reveres harmony, they are illuminated by the sacred transformation of the Yang; when the vast Dharma is followed, it encompasses the broad halo of the cosmic destiny. Thus, the monastic community assembles in the hall for the *poṣadha* to recite the precepts.
The precepts can extinguish evil and serve as the foundation for all wholesome deeds; they are the cause from which wondrous conduct arises and the root of liberation.
Upon hearing this, the śrāmaṇera leaped for joy and was filled with gladness, desiring to make an offering, yet he possessed no wealth or treasures.

Furthermore, I offer five hundred willow twigs and one thousand clean counting-sticks, respectfully presented to the pure assembly, to manifest my single-minded sincerity and to eliminate phlegm and impurities.
I humbly entreat the virtuous monks to compassionately accept these and grant their blessings.
The Demeanor of a Śrāmaṇera
